questions.text: maybe we have the Jet. as implicit and if a user overrides the Jet version then we have to handle somehow, with an error or warning about overlapping or something? Open to suggestion
questions.answer: Adopted as the new option A. Every built-in marker gets a full name, #Jet.Name, and the bare #Name means it by default, like a prelude. If you declare your own Hot, yours wins in your code, and a warning at your declaration names both. Jet's stays reachable as #Jet.Hot, and jet fix can rename yours. So a Jet release never breaks your build, and nothing is hidden for good. Two cases are errors. The first is claiming the root itself: a marker, module or import named jet. The second is relying on a shadowed built-in's permission through the bare name: if your marker is named Unsafe, Jet's unsafe gate needs #Jet.Unsafe. jet fmt writes the bare form unless a clash needs the full one, so each site has one form. Teams that want overlap to be an error can deny the warning in policy. Option C makes every overlap an error for everyone; I recommend against it, because an upgrade could then stop a build that was unambiguous. The tilde root (B) is unchanged. (The redrafted ballot is with fresh beginner and adversarial readers now; it replaces the posted text as soon as they pass.)

questions.text: Are you saying that we can just do casts by wrapping the subject value in a typed literal constructor for the type we want to cast to? like myCastedType{myCastedVar} and that this already works?
questions.answer:
Partly. `Type{value}` is how Jet builds a value of a type. With one value inside, Jet uses it whole when a parameter of that type would accept it. So it converts only where Jet already converts by itself, with a check. It is not a general cast. Tested today:

Works:
- `Float{count}` with count an Int: 4 becomes 4.0. A whole number with no exact Float, such as 9007199254740993, stops the program with error E3010.
- `I64{x}`, `F64{i}` and `U8{n}` from an Int work. `U8{n}` with n = 300 stops with E3010, since a U8 holds 0 to 255. Written as `U8{300}`, it is a compile error.

Does not work, by design:
- `String{42}`, and `Float{x}` where `x :: 2.5` (Jet reads 2.5 as an exact Decimal): compile errors.
- Your own type: `CustomerID{n}`, where CustomerID is a distinct Int, is an error; write `CustomerID.from_int(n)`. A one-field struct needs its field name: `Meters{value: i}`.
- A conversion that should report failure instead of stopping uses a named call: `U8.from_int(300)` returns a failure you can handle.

Two bugs found: `Int{f}` with f a Float, and `I32{big}` with an I64 too big for I32, compile when they should not. They print the unconverted value, and using the result crashes the compiler. A function parameter rejects both correctly. We will file them.

The ballot decides only how this one converting use is spelled: `Float{count}` (A) or `<Float>count` (B). Both do the same checked conversion; neither adds new conversions.

cards.title: [Int:V] maps miss equal Int keys >= 2^63 computed separately (silent wrong result)
cards.body: Found by MirLint2 (2026-10-01). Two Int.parse("12017618986949271521") values compare equal (a == b is true) but m.get(b) returns None after m[a] was set, and keys() prints a mangled 4611826755451994240. [String:V] keyed by the decimal text works. Repro ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/MirLint2/maptest/main.jet. Likely the map hashes the inline/boxed exact-Int representation instead of the value. The Jet compiler keys maps by MIR stable ids (u64 hashes), so it is directly exposed (Lint.jet works around it with string keys). The fix belongs in the one runtime (Prelude map hashing), which the Jet backend also calls; golden on every tier.

log.text: Closed by Main (Pip): Fixed in current code: Wide Int map keys compare by value; live probe includes negative and huge keys, has/get/iteration/replacement/removal. Evidence: crates/jet-rt/src/lib.rs:100-119; ~/.cache/jet-luna/cards/cl2/P.sh run Examples/features/collections/int_map_wide_keys.jet => exit 0, all seven recomputed keys hit, correct keys and replacement/removal

MapFix, 2026-10-01: root cause in the JIT runtime (jet-rt canonical_int_map_key kept the tagged heap pointer as the key for Ints outside i64, so equal values got different keys, iteration followed pointer order, and retain_map_key could read memory through a bogus pointer). Fixed with JetMapKey::BigInt compared by value; JIT has_key on Int and composite keys, [Int] list display, and keys() loops fixed. AOT (the path jetc0 uses) was never broken: JetMap<JetInt,V> is a BTreeMap ordered by value. Golden collections/int_map_wide_keys (wide, negative, huge keys computed separately); proofs queued. Interpreter fails loudly (E0956, no big-Int MirConstKey): frozen as obe:interpreter-retired.

MirLint2: roughly half of all MIR stable ids are >= 2^63 (u64 hashes), so every [Int:V] map keyed by MIR ids in the Jet compiler is exposed; Lint.jet keys by decimal text as a workaround; JetBackend Lower.jet keys maps by these ids and is likely affected.

cards.title: Marker registry lists `Extern` as active, but the parser retires `#Extern module` (E0060 → `#Import`)
cards.body:
`crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:203` declares `marker Extern($sites: [.Module])` as an active marker, with no `$retired` field. The parser treats it as retired: `MARKER_EXTERN_MODULE_RETIRED = "Extern"` (`crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:631`), and `#Extern module …` emits E0060 and recovers as `#Import` (`crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Items/reactive_unsafe_c.rs:302-309`). The formatter writes `#Import module` (D-ADOPT-GUEST1=A). D-META-ONE1=A makes Markers.jet the one marker vocabulary, so tools that read it (completion, `jet explain`, reflection) present a retired spelling as active.

Source: elegance audit marker-fusion evidence, 2026-10-01.
cards.plan: Make shared Prelude/Markers.jet:203 agree with ratified D-ADOPT-GUEST1=A, which the parser already implements (#Extern module -> E0060 teaching to #Import): mark the row $retired with replacement #Import. Nothing is removed; any further removal is the owner's decision.

cards.title: `#Inline(Hint)` and `#Inline(Never)` are offered by `InlineMode` but rejected by the parser
cards.body:
The marker row is `marker Inline(mode: InlineMode{.Hint}, …)` (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:42`), and the public enum `core.compiler.lang.InlineMode` has `Hint`, `Always`, `Never` (`Core/compiler/lang.jet:47-52`). The parser accepts only bare `#Inline` and `#Inline(Always)`; any other argument, including the declared default `Hint` written explicitly and `Never`, is a marker shape error (`crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Items/marker_groups.rs:1452-1465`). Ratified D-INLINE-PARAM1=A covers the soft hint and the checked `Always` promise; whether `Never` is intended is unknown, so this card needs triage.

Source: elegance audit marker-fusion evidence, 2026-10-01.
cards.plan: Jet compiler: Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Items.jet:1472-1480 recognizes only the retired InlineAlways name, so #Inline(Always) loses its checked promise; map Hint->is_inline and Always->is_inline_always. #Inline(Never) is declared in InlineMode but has no behavior: the owner decides whether Never stays (and then gets behavior) — do not remove it without that decision.

cards.title: No superlinear algorithms in the compiler: audit Compiler/ + scaling benchmark guard
cards.body: Owner directive 2026-10-01: the compiler must have no quadratic or superlinear algorithms that blow up on large programs, including rarely used features such as history capture (testing.histories). Found today: MIRRust generic_params O(functions x all instructions x depth) under history mode (and history mode was on for every AOT program), history_binding linear scan per value, emitter type/impl lookups, Cranelift dominator growth, MIR verification cloning per-block state. Deliver: (1) static audit of Compiler/ with fixes, stage-1 path first; (2) a scaling benchmark (synthetic programs at N/2N/4N/8N per axis: functions, types, closures incl. nested, enum variants, match arms, modules, literals, generic instantiations, a testing.histories user) timing every compiler phase and flagging growth faster than ~N log N; run on every release snapshot. Worker: ScalingAudit.

log.text: Closed by Main (Pip): Merged into #4319: Keep #4319; carry #4147 audit findings, N/2N/4N/8N histories/nested-closure/generic/huge-program axes and release guard into it. Evidence: #4319 deterministic work-counter scaling gate and data-structure law; #4147 scaling audit log

Superlinear3, 2026-10-01 (written, cargo check clean, unbenchmarked): causes found by perf on every scaling axis: loop-fact derivation walked the downstream region per branch (50-55% of emit on elseif1024 and enum_variants); emitter per-value queries rescanned the whole function; generic_params scanned every function per top-level function; function_row/collect_window_params linear per call; lowering searched for the current block per instruction. Fixed in Rust (MIROptimization.rs cycle-block set via iterative Tarjan + position map; MIRRust.rs cached FunctionIndex; mir.rs/tir_to_mir_stmt.rs position maps) and Jet (LoopVector.jet, Builder.jet). Jet emitter gap: Emit/Values.jet value lookups still scan per value. Not fixed: type-instance insertion linear search (types axis), prelude-call lookup, coverage_branch_id, vector emit rescans, value-match lower_if_expr recursion per arm (debug stack: ~370 arms overflows 192 MiB), memmove hotspot 25% on match1024.

MoveEmit, 2026-10-01 (written, unbuilt): last-use move pass in both compilers (Rust TIR/tir_to_mir_last_use.rs, Jet Codegen/LastUse.jet): a whole-local read of an owned local with no later use becomes a move and clears its drop flag (covers ^x and plain last uses); by-value Prelude arguments used once are taken, not cloned (removes the list-push clone); a moved match subject is destructured once for all payload bindings. New golden Examples/features/memory/last_use_moves.jet. Proofs pending: goldens (memory, collections, patterns, basics, errors), chain bench 2000/8000/32000 expected linear, JIT/interpreter/web see MovePlace where they saw ReadPlace (risk). Open: sema false E0121 on rest = [S]{..Val(^rest)} in a loop.

DeepRecursion2, 2026-10-01: Jet compiler if-chain lowering, TIR children walks and the sema switch-chain fold now read else bodies in place, one frame per arm, no copies (old recursion and DeepRecursion's loop were both quadratic through copies). E1403 ported to JetSema (close; counts per statement list). Measured Rust emit still superlinear: match emit 0.63/1.29/3.88/15.2 s at 512-4096 arms; else-if emit 4.6 s at 1024, 18.6 s at 2048. Remaining causes (both compilers): loop-fact derivation walks downstream per branch block (~45%: MIROptimization.rs derive_loop_and_vector_facts / collect_loop_region; Jet LoopVector.jet mir_pass_instruction_for_value); emitter per-query whole-function scans (~25%: history_binding, value_definition, window_parameter_value, parameter_place, value_type...); lowering block searches (~3%).

DeepRecursion2, 2026-10-01: root-cause finding: the Rust emitter that builds jetc0 deep-clones on every local read, on ^x moves (clone + drop instead of a move), on list push of temporaries and on enum payload extraction from non-window subjects; only read-param windows are zero-copy. A loop walking an N-link chain: 2000 = 1.3 s, 8000 = 47.7 s (quadratic). Both the old recursive and the new loop if-chain lowering were quadratic through this. MoveEmit (new) makes moves moves and last uses moves in both emitters; DeepRecursion2 uses window-style recursion (1 frame/arm, zero copies) meanwhile.

DeepRecursion, 2026-10-01: else-if chain lowering is now a loop in both compilers (Jet jet_codegen_lower_if + tir_stmt_children, Rust lower_if): 0 frames per arm instead of 4, so the 256-arm match no longer hits the 1024-frame E3012 limit. New cost to remove: the Jet loop copies the rest of the chain each step (quadratic in arms). The 1024-frame limit is an implementation constant (Outcome.rs:2520), not ratified; ballot draft D-STACK-BUDGET1 for later. Found, not fixed: 256-deep .trim() chain overflows the Rust checker's native stack; recursive enum values ~22 deep die with 'typed drop value recursion limit exceeded' on run/build; JetSema lacks the ratified E1403 nesting check (D-COMPILE-STACK1).

BorrowEmit, 2026-10-01: both compilers now read places rooted at a read parameter in place instead of copying them (a read parameter cannot change during the call): Let aliases and ?? bindings of such places, refutable binds and enum matches use read windows, Option/Result/enum tests and canonical equality inspect by reference, and loops over a read-param list walk it by index with a read-only alias. Write params, captures, ~ copies, mutable bindings and ^ moves still copy. Rust side passed run 7's cargo check; Jet side isocheck clean. Golden memory/read_param_borrows (mutation-after-borrow cases) added; proofs queued. Gaps: the Jet ?? window covers return/break/next/panic fallbacks only.

ScalingAudit2, 2026-10-01: Jet-side fixes (isocheck clean): each function check copied the whole environment twice incl. the registration graph (now by reference); module scope table copied per function and per branch/arm (now in place with mark/rollback and an undo log); missing-variant coverage O(variants x arms) and nested-arm grouping O(arms^2) now single passes; driver callback merge now id maps; lambda binding frames via the name index. No match-arm limit in the Jet compiler, but sema lowers an N-arm match to an N-deep if/else chain (stack depth scales with arms); biggest match in Compiler/ is 256 arms (HandleMethods.jet:1014), right at the Rust compiler's 257-arm E1403 limit. Biggest enums: THandleOp 329 variants, TBuiltinOp 220, TExprKind 119. Open: O2, O3, O6, O11, rest of O4/O5/O10.

Owner direction 2026-10-01 (on the 1.13 GB / 16.5M-line emitted jetc0): "absurd and unacceptable amount of code and size"; "We should design the jet compiler to be able to handle that ANYWAY"; fix the Rust and Jet compilers in tandem so the issue does not reappear in Jet after stage 0. Scope added: (a) shrink emission (reachable code only, compact derives, tables as data, structured emission) in both emitters; (b) the Jet compiler handles huge programs regardless: streaming output, output split into many modules/crates for parallel and incremental rustc, per-function units, linear memory; (c) the scaling guard gains a huge-program axis (millions of lines) run on every release snapshot.

ScalingAudit2, 2026-10-01: stage-1 blocker found: the Rust emitter (which builds jetc0) deep-clones read places: loops over read params/fields (names.clone(), env.a.list.clone()), Option/compare subjects on places (env.graph.clone()). In the Jet compiler, loops over graph.modules and ~123 registration_graph Option matches would copy the whole registration graph per call: quadratic in program size. Freeze exception granted (Pip): BorrowEmit makes read loops and place matches borrow in MIRRust and the Jet emitter, with goldens proving no missing copies.

ScalingAudit, 2026-10-01: stage-1-path fixes in the Jet compiler (isocheck clean): emitter index maps built once per program (~40 per-use table scans removed), window-param fixpoint made linear, lowering merge dedup O((F+N)^2) -> maps, field-symbol index, per-name sema scope index. Guard built: ~/.cache/jet-luna/scaling/ (gen.mjs 9 axes at N/2N/4N/8N, run.mjs --profile=rust|jetc flags doubling ratio > 2.4, audit-scan.mjs). First Rust report: enum-variant emission worse than cubic (1.6/7.7/51/407 s at 100-800 variants), match arms up to 5.6x per doubling and E1403 at 257+ arms, types/string literals/modules ~3.5x, generic instantiations 2.7x. 13 findings open in ~/.cache/jet-luna/status/ScalingAudit-findings.md.

cards.title: Database transactions can end unchecked: no compile-time guarantee of commit or rollback
cards.body:
Connections are safe today: every value whose type implements `Close`, including `DBConnection`, `DBScope`, `DBPool`, and `DBLease`, is closed exactly once at scope end on success, early return, error, panic, and cancellation, and moved values are closed by their new owner (D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1=A, D-SHAPE-RESOURCE2=A; `crates/jet-foundation/src/Traits.rs:2788-2809`; Jet compiler scope-end close in `Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/Builder.jet:833-838`).

Transactions are not tracked. `conn.begin()`, `conn.commit()`, and `conn.rollback()` are plain methods returning `Bool` (`Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Database.jet:38-45,61-68`). So:
- a function can begin a transaction and return on some path without committing or rolling back; the transaction then ends when the connection closes, with provider-defined behavior (whether that is a rollback is unverified);
- a failed `commit()` returns `false`, and nothing requires the caller to look at it.

D-SHAPE-RESOURCE2 says protocol success such as `commit` stays an explicit fallible operation rather than pretending automatic cleanup succeeded; today's `Bool` results and untracked transaction state fall short of that. Ignoring an effect is not the right hook: the obligation belongs to the transaction value, not to functions marked `-[DB]>`.

The owner chose (2026-10-01) to track this separately from the debts principle (#4139). Any new syntax or API needs an owner decision.

Source: elegance audit discussion, 2026-10-01.
cards.plan: Owner decision first: choose how a transaction's ending is guaranteed (for example a transaction value that must reach commit or rollback on every path, a callback-scoped transaction, or making commit/rollback results must-use). Then implement in the Jet compiler only (Rust compiler frozen); verify what each provider does with an open transaction at close.

cards.title: Marker law and marker families: one marker shape, named groups, and fused marker families
cards.body:
Owner-led elegance discussion, 2026-10-01. Agreed direction: (1) a two-tier marker law — markers written by users and libraries may read facts, add code, and reject (only ever stricter); only Jet's Prelude markers change compiler checking settings, and each states which setting it changes; (2) `derive T.X { … }` folds into marker bodies; (3) named marker groups; (4) the marker family fusions the owner listed: Codable options, Rename case, typestate arrow, CLI field options, codegen hints, Wasm export, conditional presence, job schedule, and file settings.

Each item is a separate ballot on this card so the owner can adopt any subset. Every fusion keeps every current capability; retiring an old spelling happens only if the owner ratifies it.

cards.title: `#Discriminant` and `#Untagged` on one enum are both accepted; `#Untagged` silently wins
cards.body:
Ratified D-SERDE7 gives enums three wire representations: external tagging (default), `#Discriminant(field)` internal tagging, and `#Untagged`. They are mutually exclusive, but nothing rejects both on one enum: encode and decode check `Untagged` first, so `#Discriminant` is silently ignored (`crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration/Serde.rs:1387-1412,1411-1477,1533-1635`). Jet-compiler counterpart not yet checked.

Source: elegance audit marker-fusion evidence (FuseCodec), 2026-10-01.

cards.title: MIR ids: dense per-function ids instead of 64-bit stable hashes
cards.body: ImageSize, 2026-10-01: the stage-zero compiler MIR image is 665 MB raw (2.14 GB as an escaped literal). Lossless coding (varint, string table, type interning: 7,431 unique types behind 307 MB of type trees, span interning) reaches ~216 MB; the floor is ~6.0M unique 64-bit stable-hash ids (values 1.76M, blocks 1.04M, ops 2.43M, places 0.33M) = 48 MB of incompressible id bytes plus references. Dense per-function ids (MirValueId/BlockId/OpId/PlaceId allocated by lowering) would cut the image below 50 MB and shrink every MIR consumer; must stay deterministic (stage-2 fixed point). Both compilers (TIR/mir.rs, Compiler/JetCodegen). Alternative: a body-less image if no reader needs function bodies (JIT/SourceInterpreterDeopt factory tiers are the only readers). Related: Runner.rs re-embedded the full compiler image into every native user program (fixed by ImageSize).

cards.title: Build-time type choice for generics (Zig comptime lesson), and the future of <>
cards.body:
Owner request (2026-10-01 mining run): Zig replaces `<>` generics with ordinary compile-time functions that return types (`fn List(comptime T: type) type`). Consider whether Jet's prep can unify generics and free `<>`.

Today Jet has three related mechanisms: ordinary `<T>` generics (S33, S45), const generics `struct Packet<prep N: Int>` (D-CONSTGEN1=A, D-CONSTGEN2=A, #3505, unbuilt), and opt-in type factories (#3528, D-META-OPTIN2=A). S26 says comptime never creates or selects a type, and D-META-GATE1=A stops the standard ladder at const generics.

Evidence: Zig probe Z1 shows `List(i32) == List(i32)` is true (memoized identity); Zig docs say comptime generics are duck-typed and fail only at instantiation (issue #1268). Verse writes generics as functions over types. Mojo uses `[]` parameters plus `comptime if` for type selection.

Ballot D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 decides whether Jet keeps three mechanisms or makes `<T>` sugar over one type-returning prep function, and whether `<>` survives.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1. If A wins: bounded computed aliases (type Name<...>: Bound = prep { if ... -> X else -> Y }) in Compiler/JetSema and Compiler/JetEval after #3505; amend S26, D-CONSTGEN1's rationale, and record the D-META-GATE1 boundary in one cutover; paired performance cell before ratification.

questions.text: i think the zig style is MUCH easier to read, understand, and reason about, i dont see the benefit of A other than the fact that it wouldnt require migration but we are greenfield so migration is a non issue
questions.answer:
# D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 — answer

**Owner (verbatim):** "i think the zig style is MUCH easier to read,
understand, and reason about, i dont see the benefit of A other than the fact
that it wouldnt require migration but we are greenfield so migration is a non
issue"

Agreed. Migration should not have ranked the options, and the old ballot
undersold the Zig style. I rebuilt the ballot around it. Zig style now leads
and is recommended.

**What Zig style means in Jet (option A):**

```jet
prep fn Pair(T: Type) -> Type { struct { first: T, second: T } }

prep fn Storage(T: Type, n: Int) -> Store(T) {
    if n <= 16 -> Inline(T, n) else -> Heap(T)
}

fn larger(prep T: Comparable, a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b -> a else -> b }

p :: Pair(Int){first: 1, second: 2}
print(larger(3, 9))        // 9; Jet works out T = Int
print(larger(Int, 3, 9))   // also fine
```

Generic types, picking a type by size, and generic traits all become
ordinary-looking build-time functions called with `( )`. Generic modules keep
their `module` declaration, and only their parameter list changes. `<>` goes
away. The built-in shorthands stay: `[T]`, `[K:V]`, `T?`, `[T#N]`.

**The one thing we keep from today, on purpose.** Zig checks a generic only
when someone uses it, so a mistake inside a library shows up in the user's
build (Zig issue #1268). In the new ballot, bounds like `prep T: Comparable` are
still checked once, where the recipe is written. Errors that depend on actual
values, such as an array size, still appear at the use, as they must.

**The real question left for you: A or B.** It is about calls only.

- **A:** you may leave out the type arguments when Jet can work them out:
  `larger(3, 9)`. You may also pass all of them: `larger(Int, 3, 9)`. Passing
  only some is an error. Jet decides by counting the arguments, never by
  guessing.
- **B:** exactly Zig. Every call names its types: `larger(Int, 3, 9)`,
  `xs.map(String, fn(x) -> x.to_string())`.

I recommend A, because generic calls such as `map`, `filter`, and `decode` are
some of the most common calls in Jet. B makes all of them longer for no safety
gain. C keeps `<>` and is there only so the trade-off is visible.

**Removed from the old ballot.** "Keep `<>` with no type choice" (you ruled out
migration as a reason) and "unbounded computed types". Zig-style recipes can
now build new struct shapes, so that option added nothing.

Review note for Main: substantive rewrite with a new recommendation. The
stored reader passes are labeled inherited and were not rerun, so run fresh
beginner and adversarial passes before marking it ready. The detail lists
every amended law (S26, S33/D-GENERIC-CALL1, S45, D-CONSTGEN1/2, D-GENMOD1/2,
D-PREP-FN1, D-SERDE6/16, and D-META-GATE1's use-site type-factory refusal). A
paired performance cell is still required for the `Storage`
case. SolBallotAdvisor shaped the leading-`prep`-parameter form, the bound
meaning, and the all-or-none rule.

cards.title: Narrow authority to paths, hosts, and URLs in #Caps and the manifest, enforced at runtime
cards.body:
Owner request: like EYG, narrow effects to specific domains for Net and specific files or directories for FS.

Today the rights carrier already understands qualified rights: `Authority::covers` documents `FS.Read:/data` and `Net.Connect:api.example.com` (`crates/jet-foundation/src/Authority.rs:77-141`), and plugins and process specs use `Authority.from_rights(["FS.Read:repo"])` (Docs/spec/spec.md:3989, Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1642). But `#Caps(...)` and the manifest `authority: { holds: ... }` accept only roots and leaves, and the network bridge does not compare hosts before connecting (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/NetHTTP.rs:973-990`). FS already scopes reads to explicit descriptor roots (`FSRuntimeOps.rs:28-49`).

Prior art: EYG `access.fetch.allow_get_hosts(["api.example.com"])` and `access.read_file.allow_under(["fixtures"])`; Deno `--allow-net=host`, `--allow-read=path`; WASI preopened directories; OpenBSD `unveil`.

Ballot D-AUTH-NARROW1 decides the spelling and the static/runtime split.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-AUTH-NARROW1. Then: one qualified-right grammar in #Caps and the manifest, the same rights tree (D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1), runtime checks in the shared Prelude carriers for FS paths (already descriptor-relative), Net hosts (before connect and on every redirect), and Exec paths, with static rejection when the argument is a literal outside the grant.

cards.title: Let authors raise the prep step budget for intentional long compile-time work
cards.body:
Owner request: Zig protects the compiler from infinite comptime loops with a bounded maximum and lets the author raise it.

Zig probe Z2: the default fails with `evaluation exceeded 1000 backwards branches` and a note naming `@setEvalBranchQuota`; `@setEvalBranchQuota(10000)` succeeds. Jet has a per-binding fuel budget of 10,000,000 steps (`crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Interpreter.rs:15-30`) and E0952, but the source calls the constants "not user knobs". A legitimate large table therefore cannot be built at compile time.

Ballot D-PREP-FUEL1 decides whether and where an author raises the budget.

questions.text: fuel sounds needlessly theatrical, need a more progressional name
questions.answer:
# D-PREP-FUEL1 — answer

**Owner (verbatim):** "fuel sounds needlessly theatrical, need a more progressional name"

Agreed. The new name is **step limit**. The marker is `#StepLimit(n)`:

```jet
#StepLimit(50_000_000)
CRC_TABLE :: prep { crc_table() }
// Without it: Error [E0952]: prep reached its step limit (10,000,000)
```

The name comes from Clang, which calls the same idea "constexpr steps"
(`-fconstexpr-steps=N`). It says what is counted (evaluator steps) and that the
number is a ceiling. Names I dropped: `#PrepSteps` reads like a measured count,
not a limit. `#EvalQuota` (Zig's word) hides what is counted. Lean's
`maxHeartbeats` is as much a metaphor as "fuel".

All proposed surfaces in the ballot now use the same words: the marker, the
proposed manifest key (`prep: { step_limit: n }`), the proposed E0952 message,
and the prose. The "Current" panel still quotes today's real error text, which
says "fuel"; that is what the compiler prints now. The internal constants
`FUEL_BUDGET` and `DEV_FUEL_BUDGET` would be renamed to match during
implementation. That rename needs no ballot.

I also tightened one rule the old text left vague. The marker goes only on a
prep binding, and its limit covers everything that binding runs. A `prep fn`
helper cannot raise the limit for the code that calls it. The choice itself
(A marker, B package setting, C fixed) and the recommendation (A) are
unchanged.

Review note for Main: this is a rename plus scope rules (binding-only marker,
one total limit per binding). The stored reader passes are inherited from the
earlier text and were not rerun. SolBallotAdvisor reviewed this revision and
found no blocking issue. If Main wants fresh passes for the scope rules, run
them before marking ready.

cards.title: Struct-of-arrays chosen per collection (Columns<T>), not only per type
cards.body:
Owner request: capture how Odin handles struct-of-arrays (SoA).

Odin chooses SoA on the container: `v: #soa[N]Vector3`, `#soa[]T`, `#soa[dynamic]T`, with both `v[0].x` and `v.x[0]` (probe O1). Zig chooses it with a library type, `std.MultiArrayList(T)`. Jet chooses it on the type (`#Layout(columnar)`, D-SOA1, D-SOA2A=C, whole-struct only by D-SOA2B), so one struct cannot be AoS in one place and SoA in another, and a dependency's type cannot be stored columnar. #2889 also shows the columnar path is 15x slower than AoS today.

Ballot D-SOA-SITE1 decides where the layout choice lives.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-SOA-SITE1. Then implement the chosen surface over one columnar storage implementation in Core, fix #2889 first, and add a golden showing the same struct in both layouts.

log.text: Burn-down consolidation 2026-10-04: merged into #2889; criteria carried there as [#4169]. Per-collection Columns<T> (D-SOA-SITE1=A) is the layout deliverable blocked on #2889.

Active contract: Columns<T> selects struct-of-arrays per collection and supports literal, push, index, len and ordinary struct-row iteration, with .field views. Retire the whole-struct #Layout(columnar) selection; the same struct may occur in both layouts.

Gap evidence (static source witness, not a passing test): Both sides still carry whole-struct Layout(columnar), which the ruling retires. Jet rejects columnar-list methods beyond len/is_empty/push (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Collections.jet:151-154), and canonical Rust marker source still includes Columnar as Layout (Core/compiler/lang.jet:67-70; crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:114). Rust Columns carrier exists (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/Columns.rs:69) but does not prove the per-collection source surface/full ordinary struct-row API.

cards.title: One call spelling per function: end the method/free-function dialect
cards.body:
Owner request (Odin): methods are a dangerous rabbit hole that splits a language into dialects; operator overloading is risky, though a Numeric trait is a reasonable balance.

Odin has no methods ("data should not have behaviour; use a procedure"); `f.bar()` is a field error (probe O4). Its FAQ names the dialect problem: `foo(&x)` versus `x.foo()`. Jet has methods in three places (type body, `impl`, `fn Type.method`), and D-CALLDUAL1=E lets a `#Root` free function be called as both `f(x)` and `x.f()`, and says the formatter never rewrites either. That is exactly two spellings for one call. D-UFCS1=B rejected general UFCS for that reason. Operator hooks (D-OPDEF1, D-OPMIX1, `Numeric`) stay as ratified.

Ballot D-CALL-ONE1 decides whether each function gets one canonical call spelling.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-CALL-ONE1. Then update the formatter and add the lint or rule chosen, migrate examples in one cutover, and snapshot the diagnostic.

log.text: Burn-down consolidation 2026-10-04: merged into #3452; criteria carried there as [#4170]. One call spelling per function (D-CALL-ONE1=A) is call-surface law.
All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.

cards.title: TIR Lint: re-check types after every TIR stage in the Jet compiler
cards.body:
Owner request (Simon Peyton Jones talk UBgam9XUHs0 [08:12-10:22]): keep a statically typed program from the front of the compiler to code generation, so a broken optimization shows up as a type error inside the compiler. GHC's Core Lint re-type-checks Core after passes (-dcore-lint); GHC bug reports show it catching desugarer and specializer defects.

Jet already does most of this: TIR is typed (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/mod.rs:1-18`) and MIR Lint re-derives operand and result types after every optimizer pass (Docs/spec/mir-lint.md:1-22, Compiler/JetOptimizer/Source/Verification/Lint.jet). There is no TIR verifier in either compiler (repository search for a TIR lint or verifier finds nothing), so a sema-to-TIR or TIR-to-MIR lowering bug is only caught later or never.

No owner gate: internal checker, no surface change.
cards.plan: Add a TIR Lint in Compiler/ that re-derives each TExpr's type, checks binary overflow decisions, ownership operations, and Err payload membership, and runs after sema-to-TIR lowering and before TIR-to-MIR in compiler debug builds and in CI. Seed it with a planted lowering bug to prove it fires.

cards.title: Allocation report for jet test and jet dev: leaks, double release, and unclosed resources
cards.body:
Owner request (Zig): the built-in allocator tracks leaks; Jet should get the same safety for GC-managed and non-GC memory, and the compiler should optimize with that in mind.

Zig probe Z3: `std.testing.allocator` reports a leak and fails the test; a double free aborts with traces; `DebugAllocator` reports leaks at runtime. Jet has `jet gc report` for unproven promotions (Docs/spec/observability.md:19-24), a counting `JetProgramAllocator` (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/ProgramAllocator.rs:1-26), and scope-end close for `Close` values, but no report of live arena/pool allocations at exit, `#Close` foreign handles never released, `Shared` cycles kept alive, or allocations still live at the end of a test.

No new syntax: a report under existing commands, with a registered lint code. Whether a leak fails a test by default is a separate owner choice if it arises.
cards.plan: Track live allocations per allocator family in the Prelude allocator on test and dev builds; at exit print a grouped report with allocation sites; add a registered lint diagnostic and UI snapshot; cover Arena, Bump, Pool, Fixed, foreign #Close handles, GC promotions, and Shared cycles.
cards.checkSteps: A test that leaks one Pool slot and one foreign handle prints both with allocation sites on AOT and jet run.

cards.title: Free plain owned values at their last use, not at scope end
cards.body:
Owner request (Mojo): a value is destroyed immediately after its last use.

Mojo docs: "Mojo destroys values as soon as they're no longer used" (mojolang.org manual/lifecycle/death); Lattner cites earlier release of large tensors and fewer exclusivity conflicts (talk [50:52-53:16]). cards.title: Build returned and moved values in place: a hidden-copy budget
cards.body:
Owner request (Mojo): Mojo "never gets memcpys" from moves; why, and can Jet use it?

Mojo's claim is narrower than it sounds: moves need no copy because values have identity and are not pinned, and `out` result slots let a callee build its result in the caller's memory (mojolang.org manual/values/ownership, "Transfer implementation details"; talk [53:50-55:37]). Jet has no result-slot or copy-elision contract: a read-only view entering an owning return is materialized with a clone (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/expressions.rs:9276-9313`), and #2890 shows an element-wise loop copying a whole list (473 MiB for 20M adds).

No owner gate: code generation and measurement only.
cards.plan: Count bulk copies (memcpy and clone of non-scalar values) per gauntlet cell from generated code; build large returned values in the caller's slot; make whole-value moves copy-free; set and enforce a per-cell copy budget.
cards.checkSteps: The copy counter runs on the gauntlet; #2890's loop allocates no second list.

cards.title: Define numeric and lane types in Core Jet over a small intrinsic set (Mojo's library-first structure)
cards.body:
Owner request (Mojo): Int and Float are library structs, not compiler primitives; move as much as possible into libraries so a library update brings new hardware support.

Mojo's structure (commit 99e3a880): `Int`, `UInt`, `Float64` are aliases of one parameterized `SIMD[dtype, width]` struct whose field is a KGEN MLIR value; every dunder method calls a `pop.*` operation (`std/simd.mojo:443-605,1069-1634`); literals are compile-time arbitrary-precision `IntLiteral`/`FloatLiteral`; `Bool` wraps `i1`; the prelude is an ordinary source file. The compiler keeps parsing, parameters, lifetimes, overload resolution, and lowering.

Jet's `Int` is a compiler builtin with a Rust carrier (`crates/jet-foundation/src/Numeric.rs:3070-3077`) and C ABI entry points (`CAbi.rs:239-258`). #3690 already moves Rust-native Core into Jet; this card applies the same rule to the numeric tower: the semantics live in Core `.jet` over `__core_intrinsic` operations (D-CORE-CALL1), and the compiler keeps literal typing and intrinsic lowering.

No owner gate: user-visible types, names, and behavior are unchanged; Jet's exact `Int` semantics stay.
cards.plan: List the intrinsic operations the numeric tower needs; write Int, Float, fixed-width ints, Bool, and the lane family as Core Jet types over them; delete the matching compiler special cases; prove golden parity on every tier and no gauntlet regression.
cards.checkSteps: Numeric goldens and gauntlet numeric cells are unchanged; the compiler's numeric special-case list shrinks to intrinsic lowering.

cards.title: Replace Core services (HTTP, files, processes) inside a scope, for tests and sandboxes
cards.body:
Owner request: learn from how EYG handles effects and where Jet falls short.

EYG effects are algebraic: `perform Log("x")` reaches the nearest `handle` frame, which may resume, return early, mock, or deny; unhandled effects stop with `UnhandledEffect`. Its access policies are handlers (`Allow`, `Mock`, `Deny`). Jet effects are inferred rows that are erased before code generation (Docs/spec/spec.md:1314-1329); the only substitutable capabilities are the deterministic `Clock`/`Rng` handles of D-REPLAY1. So a Jet test cannot replace `Net.HTTP` with a fake without restructuring code to pass handles.

Ballot D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 decides whether a `#Caps` scope may install a typed replacement for an effect leaf, a full algebraic-effect system, or neither. Narrowing permission stays with D-AUTH-NARROW1; a replacement can never widen authority.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-EFFECT-HANDLE1. If A wins: Core service traits (HTTPTransport, FileSystem, ProcessRunner) read from #Context slots by the shared Prelude carrier on every tier; release profiles that deny providers compile the lookup out; golden tests for a faked HTTP transport and a recorded file system.

Jet's #Context has allocator and deadline (D-CTX1). If D-EFFECT-HANDLE1 lands Core service providers in #Context, Odin's list is the checklist: logger, assertion handler, and RNG are the services tests most often replace.

cards.title: The Python-side middle ground: untyped private helpers checked per call, or a dynamic value
cards.body:
Owner request: how can Jet offer dynamic typing? The Rust side wants static types; the Python side wants dynamic. Also Roc's "auto type recognition".

Roc infers principal types for every expression with no annotations (FAQ, langref); EYG uses HM with rows and no annotations. Mojo rejects an untyped universe for now (roadmap phase 1 non-goal) and types Python values as `PythonObject` with checked conversion. Jet requires types on signatures (S-law at Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:192-203), rejects `Any` (D-ANY-JAI1=A), and offers `DataTree` for dynamic data. The 2026-09-30 Roc report put "inferring parameter types on signatures" on its avoid list; this ballot revisits that with the owner.

Ballot D-INFER-PRIVATE1 decides the middle ground.

questions.text: can we have some kind of special "untyped type"? basically like a type that has an extensible map/dict like python objects? That way it can be growable/extensible, dynamically/procedurally typed, and we can benefit from a legitimate underlying type even if it is dynamically/gradually typed at the surface
questions.answer:
# D-INFER-PRIVATE1 — answer

**Owner (verbatim):** "can we have some kind of special "untyped type"?
basically like a type that has an extensible map/dict like python objects? That
way it can be growable/extensible, dynamically/procedurally typed, and we can
benefit from a legitimate underlying type even if it is dynamically/gradually
typed at the surface"

**Yes.** Jet is close to having one already. `DataTree`, the value JSON parses
into, is a real tagged type, and its object case is a growable map. It is just
clumsy to build and read. The rewritten ballot asks you to choose how far to
take it:

```jet
row := Dyn.object()
row.price = 2.5
row.qty = 4
row.note = "sale"                 // the object grows while running
print(row.price * row.qty)        // 10.0, checked while running
total :: (row.price * row.qty).decode<Float>() ?? 0.0   // back to typed code
print(row.discount)               // stops: row has no field "discount"
```

- **A (recommended): dynamic data objects.** `Dyn` replaces `DataTree` as Jet's
  one dynamic type. Fields grow with dots. Values go in without wrappers.
  Operators are checked while running. Fields hold data only: numbers, text,
  booleans, null, lists, and nested objects. Typed code is unchanged, and
  `decode` turns a `Dyn` into a typed struct whenever you want the checks
  back. This is the "legitimate underlying type" you described: one tagged
  value, not a hole in the type system.
- **B: full Python objects.** Everything in A, plus fields that hold
  functions, structs, and handles such as open files. They are read and called
  by name while running: `row.discount = fn(p: Float) -> Float { p * 0.9 }`.
  This is the complete version of what you asked for. It costs three things.
  It adds a general `Any` type, which was rejected before (D-ANY-JAI1). Effects
  of stored functions must be checked while running. And values that must be
  finished on purpose, or borrowed references, still cannot go inside, because
  a dynamic box cannot keep their rules.
- **C: nothing new.** Keep building `[String:DataTree]` maps by hand.

A is data only, so it does not fully cover "like Python objects" if you want
methods stored on the object. That choice is yours; the ballot shows both.

**What happened to the old question.** The old ballot asked something else:
"may a private helper skip writing its parameter types?" That is a different
feature, so I moved it to its own ballot, D-INFER-HELPER1, keeping its main options (see
`D-INFER-HELPER1.split.md`). Leaving out a type does not mean `Dyn` under any
option here.

Review note for Main: substantive rewrite; the question itself changed. The
stored reader passes are labeled as belonging to the earlier ballot. Run fresh
beginner and adversarial passes before marking it ready. SolBallotAdvisor's
note (advisor/D-INFER-PRIVATE1.md) shaped the A/B payload split and B's
run-time effect, ownership, and encoding rules.

questions.text: I think the dyn type is good but what exactly are the tradeoffs against python objects? Also, I think it would still be useful to have some kind of version of the typed data tree that can be used for csv, json, yaml, etc as a "portable" format like datatree but i dont like the name data tree. It seems like dyn drops some features that datatree has but I want to have all the typed support of data tree. If that can be baked into dyn then that's fine,  but if not we need to keep data tree type but need a new name for it
questions.answer:
Short version: under option A, Dyn IS DataTree renamed and made pleasant. It keeps every DataTree feature (the same cases; JSON, TOML, YAML and CSV parse/render; pointer; patch; canonical bytes; streaming events; typed encode from structs and typed decode into structs). Nothing is dropped, so no second "portable data" type is needed. I tightened option A's text on the ballot to say that explicitly.

Trade-offs, Dyn (A) versus full Python objects (B):

What A gives that Python objects can't:
1. Portable: every Dyn value can be written to any format and read back (it is only data), so it is the interchange type for csv/json/yaml/toml/cbor.
2. Comparable and hashable by content, with a canonical byte form (signatures, caching, dedup).
3. Safe to share and send between tasks/processes; copying is cheap and well defined; nothing to close.
4. Effects stay checked at compile time: a Dyn can't hide a function that does IO.

What B adds, and what it costs:
1. You can store functions, structs and resource handles in fields and call them by name at run time (like Python).
2. Cost: those values can't be serialized, so B is no longer the portable format; you'd need A anyway for data.
3. Cost: a stored function's effects (IO, network...) are only known at run time, which breaks Jet's static effect checking unless every call goes through a run-time permission check.
4. Cost: Dyn becomes move-only (it may own handles that must be closed), equality/hashing stop being defined, and every field access is a dynamic dispatch (slower).

Recommendation: A. Behaviour belongs in structs, traits and closures, which stay statically checked; data that needs to be shapeless goes in Dyn. If later you want runtime-attached behaviour, it can be a separate, explicit opt-in type rather than making the portable data type unsafe.

One gap in both today: DataTree has no case for raw bytes or dates/times (CBOR byte strings, TOML datetimes). If you want 'all typed support' to include those, that is a small follow-up question: add Bytes and DateTime cases to Dyn.

cards.title: Decode typed data straight from bytes, without building a DataTree first
cards.body:
Owner request (Roc): Roc's "excellent JSON solver thing" and automatic value handling.

The Roc feature is type-directed parsing: the format supplies primitive operations and the target type supplies the shape, so `Json.parse` fills a record with no hand-written decoder and no intermediate tree (Roc commit e79b7f85, `docs/langref/parsers.md:3-39`; fixtures `test/cli/BoxyDerivedJsonParsers.roc`). Jet's typed path is trait-based (`Decode.decode(tree: DataTree)`, Docs/spec/spec.md:506-510): text is parsed into a `DataTree` and then decoded, which allocates the whole tree first.

No owner gate if the public `decode<T>` surface stays as ratified: this changes how derived decoders run, not what users type.
cards.plan: Generate derived decoders that read the format's token stream directly into the target type, keep `DataTree` for dynamic use, keep error paths and field names identical, and measure against the current path and serde_json on the gauntlet JSON cell.
cards.checkSteps: Decoding a 50 MB JSON array into typed records allocates no DataTree and beats the current path; error messages are unchanged.

cards.body:
Found 2026-10-01 by live probe J1 (mining run, binary built from HEAD 1aca7cfe2).

Source:
```jet
fn spin() -> Int {
    i := 0
    loop i >= 0 -> i += 1
    return i
}
X :: prep { spin() }
fn run() { print("{X}") }
```

cards.title: Release builds pass target-cpu=native, against the ratified baseline default (D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B)
cards.body:
Found 2026-10-01 by the adversarial review of D-CPU-DISPATCH1 (mining run).

Actual: `Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet:141` builds every release binary with `-C target-cpu=native`. A binary built on a new server can therefore crash with an illegal instruction on an older machine.

Expected: D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B (ratified): with no CPU or feature flags, every build, including a host build, uses the selected target's portable CPU baseline; explicit `--cpu` and `--features` opt into advanced instructions, and such an artifact refuses to start when a required feature is missing. AOT, JIT, and interpreter consume the same resolved profile.

Note for the performance gate: matched peers must be built with the same CPU policy, so gauntlet cells that relied on native codegen need re-measurement.

cards.title: Write bit fields the way binary patterns read them: byte-building holes and packed structs
cards.body:

Zig packed structs, Odin bit_field, and Erlang bit syntax (which both matches and builds) are the prior art. Probe (2026-10-02): writing an IPv4 header start needs hand arithmetic. cards.title: Cleanup that runs only when a function fails (Zig errdefer)
cards.body:
Zig's errdefer runs cleanup only on error exits, beside the acquisition. questions.text: this ballot is very unclear to me and the syntax looks invented not existing, not clear about it. not even sure what exactly this ballot is asking
questions.answer:
# D-DATATREE-PATH1 — answer

**Owner (verbatim):** "this ballot is very unclear to me and the syntax looks
invented not existing, not clear about it. not even sure what exactly this
ballot is asking"

You were right on both counts. Here is the plain question.

**The question.** When a program reads JSON *without* declaring a struct for
it, should it be able to write `tree["user"]["name"]`, the same `[ ]` indexing
Jet already uses for lists (`xs[1]`) and maps (`m["key"]`)?

That is all it asks. Reading JSON into a struct (`json.decode<User>(raw)`) is
the main path and does not change.

**Today (spellings from the repository's example files):**

```jet
tree :: json.parse(raw) ?? panic("parse")
user :: &tree.field("user") ?? panic("user")
name :: &user.field("name") ?? panic("name")
print(name.text() ?? "anon")
tag :: json.pointer(tree, "/user/tags/1") ?? panic("tag")   // JSON Pointer path
```

**Recommended (A):**

```jet
tree :: json.parse(raw) ?? panic("parse")
print(tree["user"]["name"].text() ?? "anon")
print(tree["user"]["tags"][1].text() ?? "none")
print(tree.get("user")?.get("nickname")?.to_text() ?? "anon")  // a miss gives None
```

`tree["user"]` behaves exactly like `m["user"]` on a map. If the key is missing,
the program stops with a report that quotes the expression, for example
`tree["user"]["nickname"]: no key "nickname"`. `.get` gives an optional
instead, so you can chain with `?.`, as you already can with lists and maps.

**What I fixed in the ballot.**

- The old "current" example dropped the `&` that real code uses. It now copies
  the spellings in `datatree_accessors.jet` and `json_pointer.jet`.
- The old option B, `tree.path("user.name")`, was invented. Jet already has a
  path reader that follows a published standard (RFC 6901, JSON Pointer):
  `json.pointer(tree, "/user/name")`. I removed the invented option. The ballot
  is now A (add indexing) against B (keep today's tools, including
  `json.pointer`).
- Both options now show the same program with the same outputs.
- The lesson opens with what `DataTree` is and what stays unchanged. The detail
  covers the edge cases: wrong kind, JSON `null` versus a missing key, negative
  indexes, no `"0"`-to-`0` conversion, and writing through `[ ]`.
- It says plainly what A does not do: with JSON of unknown shape, a mistyped key
  is still found only when the program runs. Typed decode is the way to get
  compile-time checks.

**Related.** Your "untyped type" question on D-INFER-PRIVATE1 is about a
dynamic object type. If that ballot adds one, it uses this same `[ ]` rule, so
the two answers fit together.

Review note for Main: short profile, as before. SolBallotAdvisor reviewed it.
Its fixes are applied: the `&`, the `FieldError!` spelling, the same leaf
conversion in both options, the optional flattening source, and no
over-claims. The probe facts (E0505, E2402) are carried over from the earlier
ballot and were not rerun, because no debug `jet` build was available in this
session.

cards.title: Reject invisible bidirectional-control characters in source (Trojan Source, CVE-2021-42574)
cards.body:
Roc forbids literal bidi control characters in source, shows them visibly in diagnostics, and keeps escapes for runtime data (roc docs/langref/strings.md:209-229). No Jet lexer, spec, or test mentions bidi controls (repository search of Compiler/JetLexer, crates/jet-lexer, Docs/spec on 2026-10-02). Trojan Source lets reviewed code differ from compiled code, which undermines Jet's auditability pillar.

No owner gate: a security diagnostic consistent with ratified UTF-8 source rules.

cards.title: Accelerate the ratified hardened profile and #Unsafe sentries with memory-tagging hardware (Arm MTE, CHERI)
cards.body:
Jet already ratified the software side: D-MEM-SENTRY1 (dev sentries for #Unsafe gates), D-HARDENED1 (--profile=hardened checks only #Unsafe islands and FFI edges, card #1888 done), and D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 (contain:/harden: and jet inspect guarantees).

Hardware can now do part of that work: Arm MTE tags allocations and pointers (Armv8.5+, shipping in Pixel 8+ and recent Arm servers); CHERI/Morello turns pointers into bounded capabilities; PAC/BTI and Intel CET protect control flow. Odin and Zig expose sanitizers per build. Nothing in Tower measures whether the hardened profile, sentries, or contain: fences could use MTE tags or CHERI capabilities to cut their cost.

Research and measurement only; any new flag, profile name, or policy value becomes a ballot.

cards.title: E0116 Fix gives rejected advice for a `?? { print(...) }` fallback on a unit-fallible call
cards.body:
Probe (2026-10-02, jet run): handling the failure of a unit-fallible call by printing is a natural first attempt.

```jet
save("") ?? { print("save failed") }
```

It fails with E0116 "`print` doesn't hand back a value", whose Fix says: "Inside an arm, wrap the call in `{ … }`". The call is already inside `{ … }`, so the advice repeats the rejected form. The law (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1701-1705) says a `?? { … }` block ends with one bare value or a diverging tail; shipped examples end with `unit()` (Examples/features/collections/sort_key_contract.jet:65-68) or `return` (Examples/features/io/files_set_mode.jet:22-25).

Found while writing the D-DEFER-FAIL1 ballot.
cards.plan: In the self-hosted checker's diagnostic for a `?? { … }` block whose tail is a unit call, emit a Fix naming the two legal tails: end the block with `unit()` or with `return`. Keep E0116's generic Fix for other sites. Update the UI snapshot.
cards.checkSteps: jet check on `save("") ?? { print("save failed") }` shows a Fix that mentions `unit()` and `return`.

cards.title: Measure state-machine dispatch loops against C switch and Zig labeled-switch continue
cards.body:
Zig's labeled switch with `continue :sw next_state` lowers state machines and bytecode interpreters to direct jumps between prongs (threaded dispatch), which is why Zig's own tokenizer uses it. Jet writes the same program as `loop` plus an `if state == { … }` table; nothing measures whether that lowers to a jump table or to threaded dispatch on AOT and the JIT.

Performance-surface law (AGENTS.md): no new surface until the plain spelling is shown to lose in a paired cell. This card is that measurement.
cards.plan: Write a paired cell: a 30-state tokenizer and a small bytecode VM in plain Jet versus C (switch and computed goto) and Zig (labeled switch). Inspect generated code. If plain Jet loses beyond the gate, file a ballot for a surface or an optimizer card; if it wins, close with the receipt.

cards.title: #Todo goals list valid fits: in-scope values and functions of the expected type (GHC typed holes)
cards.body:
D-TOOL2 ships `#Todo` as a typed goal: it compiles anywhere and stops at run time with file, line, and expected type (Examples/features/tooling/todo_hole.jet). GHC's typed holes go one step further: the compiler lists the in-scope bindings and functions whose type fits the hole, and EYG/Unison editors keep such holes as first-class gaps. A Jet learner sketching code gets the type but not the candidates.

No new syntax: this extends what `jet check` and the LSP report for an existing `#Todo`.

cards.title: Tail-recursion-modulo-cons: build lists recursively without growing the stack
cards.body: Roc (and OCaml 4.14+) compile `f(x) = x :: f(rest)`-style recursion, where the recursive call sits inside a constructor, into a loop that fills the result in place. Jet's beginner surface encourages recursion (Examples/features/basics/recursive_functions*), but only plain tail calls are loops; a recursive list builder grows the stack and can overflow on large inputs.
cards.plan: Measure stack depth and time for a recursive list builder on AOT and jet run. If it overflows or loses, implement the transformation in MIR (D-TIER-FORM1) so every tier shares it; prove with a golden example on 1M elements.

cards.title: Core coverage gate: every public Core function has a doc example and a test
cards.body: Hare's stdlib mandate is that every module is documented and tested before inclusion. Jet has I5 (every feature has a golden example) and doctests (D-DOC-TESTS, Examples/features/comptime/doctests.jet), but nothing reports public Core functions that have neither a doc example nor a test. Core has ~40k lines across 40+ modules.

cards.title: Investigate conditional trait implementations for generic types (impl for Pair<T> only when T has the trait)
cards.body: Mojo (conditional conformance), Rust (`impl<T: Display> Display for Pair<T>`), and Swift all let a generic type implement a trait only when its parameters do. Jet auto-derives built-in traits when every field qualifies (Docs/spec/spec.md:494-502), which covers the common case for derivable traits. No spec text or example shows a hand-written trait implemented conditionally on a generic type, and the dedupe sweep found no Tower record.

cards.title: jet publish proposes the semver bump from the public API and effect diff
cards.body: Roc's `roc bump` (and Rust's cargo-semver-checks, Elm's `elm bump`) computes the required version bump from the public API diff. Jet already keeps API and effect snapshots for compatibility (Docs/spec/spec.md:3305; ApiFreeze E1218/E2601), so `jet publish` can say 'this is a breaking change: needs 2.0.0' instead of trusting the written version.
cards.plan: Compare the package's public API and effect rows against the last published snapshot; classify as patch/minor/major; fail publish when the written version is too small, with a Fix naming the right version.

cards.title: JIT miscompiles Option.map: treats the result-arena handle as packed 0/payload+1 (returns payload+1)
cards.body: Sol review (SolOptMap), 2026-10-02, VERIFIED on night11. crates/jet-jit/src/Collections.rs:4505-4516 checked_option_map treats the Optional receiver as packed 0/payload+1, but it is a 1-based result-arena handle: the callback runs on handle-1 and returns callback_bits+1; consumers (functions_compile.rs:6641-6743, :5561-5575) decode it as an arena handle. Also: record identity ICEs, Int add returns -1, and an absent Optional still runs a printing Never! callback on the JIT. cards.title: Failure inference: a call inside a loop expression makes the enclosing function implicitly fallible
cards.body: GateFix, 2026-10-02: in parser_parse_function, `guest_import :: loop applied in modifiers.markers { ... break true } ?? false` calls an unannotated, actually infallible helper; the Rust checker's failure inference (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/mod.rs solve_inferred_failure/body_failure_edges) counted the call as a direct failure source (loop expression checked like a lambda), so the whole parser chain up to parse_lexed became implicitly Err and callers got E0403. Root fix: infer the helper's failure from its body (it has no fallible operation) rather than treating calls in loop expressions as failure sources; mirror in Jet sema.

cards.title: Use proven purity to skip memory checks and counts on data that existed before the call
cards.body: Mining run 2026-10-02 (Vale regions: video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UavYVf0UEoc 38:20-44:16; https://verdagon.dev/blog/zero-cost-borrowing-regions-overview §3-6; https://verdagon.dev/blog/first-regions-prototype 'The Benchmarks'). Inside a pure call, everything that existed before the call is frozen, so the compiler can skip generation checks, alias checks, and count updates on it. Vale's prototype removed every generation check and matched bounds-check-only speed on one workload (1.18x vs no-bounds unsafe for both). Jet already proves purity (`fn ... -[]>`, Examples/features/effects/pure.jet), and already pays these runtime costs: Pool<T> generation checks (MathTaskMem.rs checked_get), D-MEMREF-EXCL1=A alias checks, and counted sharing under D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A and D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A. A grep of crates/ and Compiler/ finds no code that uses purity to drop any of them. This is an optimization under ratified law (D-AUTOPIN1=A, D-DENY-COST1=A): it changes cost, never meaning. Vale reports a read-only function is compiled twice, one copy for frozen inputs.
cards.plan:
1. Mark values that existed before a proven-pure call as frozen for the call's duration in MIR facts.
2. Skip Pool generation checks, alias checks, and count updates on frozen values; keep them on values created inside the call.
3. Report each skipped check through `jet inspect choices` (D-AUTOPIN1).
4. Add a paired performance cell: the same Pool-heavy read workload with and without `-[]>`, under the strict comparator.

cards.title: Investigate isolating native foreign code from Jet memory (separate stack, copied data, opaque handles)
cards.body: Mining run 2026-10-02 (Vale Fearless FFI, https://verdagon.dev/blog/fearless-ffi). Vale keeps safe and unsafe memory apart: foreign code runs on its own stack, data crosses by copy, handles given to C are scrambled generational references checked on return, Vale allocations come from a separate address range, and a dependency can be sandboxed in WebAssembly or a subprocess. Status in the source: copying and scrambled handles done; separate stacks prototyped on macOS only; heap separation and sandboxing unfinished. Jet already gates FFI per package through authority (Examples/features/lowlevel/ffi.jet:4) and has WASM sandbox packages (spec section 'Sandboxed WASM packages'). Evidence gap: this run did not establish how Jet passes Jet-owned memory to native extern code today, so a C bug's blast radius into Jet memory is unmeasured. Any new surface (for example a per-extern isolation marker) needs a ballot after the evidence exists.
cards.plan:
1. Map how each extern form (rust, c, inline c) receives Jet values today: copy, borrow, or raw pointer.
2. Write one probe per form where foreign code writes past its argument, and record what Jet memory it can reach.
3. Estimate the cost of a separate foreign stack and copied boundary data with a paired cell.
4. If a user-visible choice remains, raise a short ballot with the measured options.

cards.title: Decide how a live link behaves when its target owes a duty (#SingleUse / declared debt)
cards.body: Mining run 2026-10-02 (Vale/Valen). Two ratified rules meet in one case. D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A: when the compiler cannot prove a link's owner outlives the link, the target moves into counted memory and stays alive while any link remains. D-LIN1: a #SingleUse value must be consumed exactly once, and dropping it is E0140. If the target of such a link owes a duty, the last link to go would drop it with the duty undone. Vale states the same conflict: 'We can't put a linear type into an Rc because Rc throws away its contents when the last alias disappears' (https://verdagon.dev/blog/linear-types-borrowing, 'Addressing the Drawbacks'); its answer keeps one owning reference that settles the duty and makes every other reference a generation-checked link that never extends the lifetime (https://verdagon.dev/blog/generational-references). Jet already uses that check for Pool Ids (Examples/features/memory/pool_stale_id.jet). Link build status lives on #3645. Ballot D-LINK-DEBT1.
cards.plan: After ratification: encode the chosen rule in sema for link targets whose type owes a duty, add the matching diagnostic or runtime stop with UI snapshot and example, and prove it on jet check, jet run, AOT, and the interpreter when links ship (#3645).

cards.title: Replay concurrent runs exactly: record task message and lock order in .jetproof-replay
cards.body: Mining run 2026-10-02 (Vale perfect replayability: video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UavYVf0UEoc 56:12-58:27; https://verdagon.dev/blog/perfect-replayability-prototyped 'Handle Multi-threading' and its linked design: each channel message carries a hidden sequence id the receiver records, and each mutex keeps a version and read count; replay waits for the recorded message or version). Jet's ratified capture (D-JREPLAY1=A, D-RUN-RECORD1=A) records Time by default and Time/Rand/Io/Net under --capture-sensitive. It does not record which message a task received first or which task took a lock first, so a race that depends on task interleaving cannot be replayed. core.testing world gives deterministic scheduling in tests only (Examples/features/concurrency/deterministic_world.jet). Ballot D-REPLAY-ORDER1.
cards.plan: After ratification: add the chosen ordering records to the capture adapters for channels, locks, Shared guards, and task joins; replay waits on the recorded order; prove a two-task race replays identically on jet run and AOT.

cards.title: Jet compiler hashes used ^ (power, D-EXPSEM1) where XOR was intended
cards.body: HashFix, 2026-10-02: stable_id (MIR/MIR.jet), MIR digest lanes (MIR/Digest), Derivations.jet and Types/TupleNames.jet implement FNV-1a / SipHash with `^`, which in Jet is exponentiation (D-EXPSEM1), not xor. Effects: IDs differ from the Rust reference's FNV values (stable_id("mir-function","main"): Jet 10808190364421781419 vs Rust 1771420404053674483), and the intermediate values are astronomically large big integers (jetc0 spent most of its hello run in BigInt arithmetic; SipHash-style chains would effectively hang). Fix in progress: U64 wrapping with Jet's xor operator, matching the Rust reference values; sweep Compiler/ and Core/ for other `^` meant as xor. Follow-up worth a lint: `^` with a hash/bitmask context (mask, shift, rotate) is almost certainly a mistake.

log.text: Closed: criterion met with the cited receipt; independently re-verified (Sol SolCardsVerify + Pip).

HashFix, 2026-10-02: fixed: stable_id, MIR digest lanes, Derivations, TupleNames (U64 wrapping, real xor; values equal the Rust reference on 11 probes) and SHA256.jet (U32 wrapping; equals sha256sum on 5 vectors). Sweep: no other xor-meant ^ in Compiler/ or Core/. Remaining outside scope: Jetpack/Store/Tests/Broker.jet:197,251 `Int.from_u8(b) ^ 1` meant as a bit flip (power 1 is a no-op, so the corruption test corrupts nothing). Also: night11 jet run (JIT) segfaults on U64 wrapping_mul in a loop (rustc path fine).

criteria.text: Hash and digest code uses XOR (~|) with wrapping fixed-width arithmetic where the reference does, and produces the reference values
criteria.evidence: MIR/MIR.jet stable_id, MIR/Digest lanes, Derivations.jet, Types/TupleNames.jet use U64 wrapping with ~|; Hash/SHA256.jet uses U32. Probes: 11 hash values byte-identical to the Rust reference (HashFix new.txt vs ref.txt) and 5 SHA256 vectors identical to sha256sum (sha/out.txt vs ref.txt).

cards.title: Known-value module constants are emitted as getter functions; uses should fold to MIR constants
cards.body: Owner, 2026-10-02: `OS_PAGE_SIZE :: prep { 4096 }` (and plain `NAME :: 4096`) compiles to a Rust getter `#[inline] pub fn OS_PAGE_SIZE() -> JetInt { JetInt::from_i64(4096) }`, and every use is a call into an Option slot, a clone, then JetInt arithmetic; list constants like `X64_CALLER_SAVED_POOL :: prep { [Int]{1, 2, 6, ...} }` rebuild a vec! at every use. Immutable module constants with a known compile-time value (scalars, strings, small tables) should be substituted as MIR constants at every use site, so the optimizer folds them further; larger tables become static data built once; the getter/address form exists only for #Static (D-CONSTMARK1). Both compilers (MIR-level, backend-agnostic).

cards.title: core.data.plot and core.perf calls crash with exit 139 (segfault) on the default run tier
cards.body: Found by Sol SolExampleCoverage (2026-10-02), night12 release jet, default `jet run`: (1) `use core.data.plot as p; fn run() { print(p.bar_text(["a","b"],[1,2])); print(p.line_text(["a","b"],[1,2])) }` exits 139 with no output; (2) `use core.perf as p; fn run() { print("{p.is_full(p.of(1.0))}:{p.is_low(p.of(0.1))}:{p.scale(p.of(0.5),10)}") }` exits 139 with no output. A segfault from safe Jet code violates I1 (memory safety) regardless of tier. Work: reproduce on AOT and default run, find the faulting route (likely a host/runtime ABI mismatch for these Core modules), fix, and add goldens for both modules (I5: neither has an example). Also from the same audit: ratified $phase/$program facts give E0107, @SOURCE/@TYPES give E0102, and prep-number parameters give E0390: check against the decision ledger (~/.cache/jet-luna/sol/decisions/RATIFIED-STATE.md) and card separately if untracked.

Triage evidence: Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreCallRows.jet registers Core runtime routes; crates/jet-jit/src/jit/functions_compile.rs:16969-16985 marshals Core host results; accepted plot/perf crashes lack proven root.

Fourth shape (RtW7-SHA256, night12): masked narrowing braces U8{x & 0xff} (from U32) and U32{y & mask} (from U64) are accepted by sema and then the emitter drops the constructor, leaving u32/u64 where u8/u32 are expected: rustc E0308 (generated unit.rs:134331, 134659, 136259). Sources use the D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 conversions (U8.from_u32 / U32.from_u64 on masked values) instead.

Another shape (CompW2-AST-CODEC, night12): narrowing brace F32{value} from a Float is accepted by sema and then fails rustc (expected f32, found f64; ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/CompW2-AST-CODEC/.jet/build/scalars.rs:137308, scalars.rustc.log). Sema must reject every narrowing brace (Int{Float}, U8{U64}, F32{Float}) with the explicit-conversion fix text; checked programs never reach rustc errors (I2).

Same family, integer narrowing (CLI-49 via PortLead-9): sema accepts U8{count >> (shift * 8) & U64{255}} (a U64 narrowed through the U8 typed head, illegal under D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 / D-DOTCTOR3: typed heads take widening only), then the emitter pushes a u64 into a Vec<u8>: rustc E0308, exit 101. Repro ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/PortW13-CLI-49/CLI-49/u8-u64-failing-source.txt (unit.rs:205260, log there). Sema must reject every narrowing typed-head conversion (Float->Int, U64->U8, ...) with the destination-owned checked conversion as the fix.

Absorbs #4235 (dup): Same unsafe typed-head Float-to-Int root; keep compiler I1 enforcement plus fmt caller migration on 4264. Evidence: Core/text/fmt.jet:206; card 4264 log explicitly names remaining fmt Float-body Int{} site

Same defect class, F32 (PortW5-CLI-23 on jet-debug-snapshot206):  with a Float variable type-checks but emits an f64 into Option<f32> (rustc E0308, exit 101). The typed head must either be rejected in sema (like Int{Float}) or lower through the checked F32.from_float.

Root cause (CardLead writer CB-PLOTPERF, 2026-10-02): Core code wrote Float-to-Int narrowing as a typed head Int{float_expression}. The Rust checker accepts it (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerInfer/expr.rs:6169-6170 exempts numeric mismatches; :6219 returns the head type with the Float body unchanged), producing an invalid exact-Int carrier that segfaults at run time (exit 139 reproduced). Core fix in the cards-burn worktree: six sites in Core/data/plot.jet, Core/perf/perf.jet, Core/math/stats.jet, Core/data/sketch/hll.jet migrated to Int.from_float with explicit failure handling, plus goldens math/plot_text and math/perf_fidelity (replicas pass; real goldens owed after an embedded-Core rebuild). Remaining Float-body Int{} sites: Core/data/data.jet:694,1321,1445,1457,1463, Core/text/fmt.jet:206. The compiler-side I1 defect (typed head must reject a Float body, in both compilers) remains open on this card: do not close on the Core migration alone.

cards.title: Close Canvas target, session and devtools registration lifecycle
cards.body:
Ratified contract scope; no new ballot or default is authorized.


**Scope:** Panel registration and typed devtools events; How should a user open Canvas?; How should Canvas choose its target and local endpoint?; How should Canvas share a session with app dev servers?

**Decision IDs:** D-DX-PLUGIN1, D-CANVAS-CMD1, D-CANVAS-TARGET1, D-CANVAS-SESSION1

**Acceptance criteria / missing boundary:**

- **D-CANVAS-CMD1:** Use `jet dev <source> --canvas`; Canvas is visibly a lens on the dev session; Plain dev stays terminal-only; The command is longer than a new verb.
  - **Gap witness:** PARTIAL: Rust: full ruled behavior could not be established; source search and checked front-door inventory are not an executed feature receipt. Jet port: the executable front door dispatches only help, explain, check and build (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:491-506); this decision's command path is refused by jet_cli_not_ported at :94-102, not implemented by its help/registry row.
- **D-CANVAS-SESSION1:** The app server and Canvas control host use separate listeners but one resident session; App routes stay fully customizable; Canvas never reserves paths in the application.
  - **Gap witness:** PARTIAL: Rust: full ruled behavior could not be established; source search and checked front-door inventory are not an executed feature receipt. Jet port: the executable front door dispatches only help, explain, check and build (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:491-506); this decision's command path is refused by jet_cli_not_ported at :94-102, not implemented by its help/registry row.
- **D-CANVAS-TARGET1:** Canvas always uses a Jet-owned loopback control host; The operating system selects a free port; `--canvas-port` is an expert override; The program target stays independent.
  - **Gap witness:** PARTIAL: Rust: full ruled behavior could not be established; source search and checked front-door inventory are not an executed feature receipt. Jet port: the executable front door dispatches only help, explain, check and build (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:491-506); this decision's command path is refused by jet_cli_not_ported at :94-102, not implemented by its help/registry row.
- **D-DX-PLUGIN1:** An exported #DevPanel function receives package-scoped typed state reduced from authorized jet.devtools.v1 publications, each devtools.publish(family,event,value: expr,field: .name) feeding a declared field; missing feeds warn and defaults/optionals support first render. Panels and their sole-callers compile out of release, release calls to panels error, credential/PII sinks require scrubbing, and third-party panels default to denied unless explicitly allowed.
  - **Gap witness:** PARTIAL — Rust Bundle.rs:85-86 caches typed devtools publications and crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/DevtoolsPanelCatalog.rs supplies panel catalog. Jet Core/devtools/devtools.jet is only 705 bytes and full package-scoped field-fed panel/release/credential enforcement was not established in port.


Effective-scope corrections:


All named tests/goldens below are REQUIRED delivery artifacts, proposed here unless an existing owner already names them; none was executed by this audit. Each runs the production Jet path, records compiler/source/provider identity, asserts exit/diagnostic/output or real side effects, and fails if the owning implementation is bypassed. Registry presence, mocks and fixed echo output cannot satisfy behavioral criteria. Unavailable hosts and inconclusive measurement cells remain open.

4. [D-CANVAS-SESSION1] The app server and Canvas control host use separate listeners but one resident session; App routes stay fully customizable; Canvas never reserves paths in the application. Owning evidence: PARTIAL: Rust: full ruled behavior could not be established; source search and checked front-door inventory are not an executed feature receipt.
